answer.label: Spurgeon’s illustration — later compressed wording
answer.sourceLine: The Spurgeon Library calls this a misquote while confirming Spurgeon used the lion illustration. Elliot Ritzema reproduces three longer versions about spreading the Bible or preaching the gospel. The display compresses those ideas and should be marked as a paraphrase, not presented as Spurgeon’s exact published wording.

author.name: Charles Haddon Spurgeon
author.heading: About Charles Haddon Spurgeon
author.bio: Charles Haddon Spurgeon was a British Baptist preacher associated with London’s Metropolitan Tabernacle. His sermons and devotional books reached readers far beyond his congregation. Collections such as The Salt-Cellars also transmitted proverbs, so a phrase appearing in his books need not be his invention.

context.heading: The setting behind the words
lead: Spurgeon’s longer illustrations compare defending the Bible or gospel with guarding a caged lion. He urges listeners to spread or preach the message rather than merely defend it. The compressed internet version preserves that rhetorical idea while changing the sentences. Spurgeon Library wording correction ↗
